title: Tables
explanation: A food truck tracks a day of sales. Right now it's just cells. Turning it into a **Table** gives it a name, built-in filter arrows and striped rows, and lets formulas use column **names** like Sales[Revenue] instead of cell addresses like E2:E9. Analysts use tables because the formulas are easier to read and harder to break.

tasks.prompt: Turn the data into a Table. Select A1:E9, then right-click and choose Insert Table (or use the Table button in the toolbar).
tasks.teach: In real Excel the shortcut is **Ctrl+T** (⌘+T on Mac), but in a browser that opens a new tab, so here use the menu instead. Include the header row: the headers become the table's **column names**.
hints: Select from A1 to E9, including the headers, then right-click and choose Insert Table.
The data should get striped rows and filter arrows.

tasks.prompt: The table is called Table1. Give it a better name: right-click any cell inside the table, choose Rename Table, and call it Sales.
tasks.teach: A good table name makes formulas readable. Names can't have spaces, can't start with a number, and must be unique.
hints: Right-click a cell inside the table (not outside it), then Rename Table.
Type Sales, with a capital S.

tasks.prompt: In E2, work out Tacos' revenue using column names: type =[@Units]*[@Price]. If it doesn't fill down by itself, copy it down to E9.
tasks.teach: Inside a table, **[@Units]** means "the Units value in this same row". So `=[@Units]*[@Price]` works in every row, and it reads like plain English.
hints: Type =[@Units]*[@Price] in E2 and press Enter.
If the other rows stay empty, copy E2 down to E9.
tasks.answer: =[@Units]*[@Price] in E2, filled down to E9

tasks.prompt: In H1, add up all the revenue using the table name: =SUM(Sales[Revenue]).
tasks.teach: **Sales[Revenue]** means "the whole Revenue column of the Sales table". If rows are added to the table later, the formula includes them automatically.
hints: Table name, then the column name in square brackets.

tasks.prompt: In H2, work out the average price using the table name.
hints: Same pattern as H1, with AVERAGE and the Price column.

tasks.prompt: Last one: tables come with filter arrows built in. Use the arrow on Category to show only Drinks.
hints: Click the arrow on B1 and keep only Drinks ticked.
3 rows should be left: Horchata, Lemonade and Soda.

recap: A Table gives your data a name, filter arrows and striped rows. [@Column] means this row's value, and TableName[Column] means the whole column, so formulas read like plain English.
